title: The pace of a sehaj path
word: The pace of a sehaj path
hookLine: round-ups in a savings app add up; a page a day reaches the end of the Granth too
tomorrow: and on the very last page, what happens?

lines: A PAGE A DAY: ABOUT FOUR YEARS.
FIVE A DAY: UNDER A YEAR.
cards: A savings app rounds every coffee up to the next dollar and tucks away the change. Nobody notices a few cents. A year later, there's a number in there that surprises people.
Now the Granth. Its pages are called Angs, and the standard printing runs to Ang 1430. Yesterday's question: a page a day, how long until the end?
Just under four years. Five pages a day, and you finish in under a year. Which raises the real question: is slow a problem?

teach.b: The Granth's own answer comes from Sheikh Farid, a Sufi saint whose verses sit in it. In paraphrase: make patience your bow, patience your bowstring, patience your arrow, and the Creator won't let it miss.
Patience isn't waiting around. It's the whole weapon.
So the right pace is the one you can keep, the one that turns into a habit instead of a sprint you abandon. A page a day isn't slow. It's steady.
Now a neighbor who says it in its own words.
In the Buddhist Dhammapada, in Max Müller's 1881 English: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled."
Shared ground: little by little gets there. Drops fill the pot; pages reach the end. And one honest difference.
In the Dhammapada, the pot is a person filling up with good they gather by their own deeds.
In Farid's lines, the archer is patient, but it's the Creator who keeps the arrow true, and a sehaj path fills a reader with the Guru's Word, not with their own.
Same steady drip, different picture of where the filling comes from. Something to repeat tonight: two old traditions, far apart, both say the slow way isn't the lesser way. It's how the pot fills.

how: People reading a sehaj path choose a daily amount that fits their life, a page or several, and keep a marker at their place in the Guru Granth Sahib or in a gutka or app until they reach the end.

games.q: what does “the pace of a sehaj path” mean?
o: a fixed speed every reader has to keep up
how long a nonstop reading of it takes
how much you read each day to reach the end

games.q: page by page — tap the pairs.
p: patience is the bow and the arrow
drops of water fill the pot

s: reading slowly means you haven't really done a sehaj path
the right pace is the one you can keep; a page a day still reaches the end.
Sheikh Farid's verses, a Sufi saint's, are part of the Granth
his line on patience as bow, string and arrow is in it.
the Dhammapada says a water-pot is filled by falling drops
in Max Müller's 1881 English: even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled.

games.q: your best friend Maya says she'd rather read a whole long book in one summer and be done with it. you're doing a page a day. what does Farid's line say about pace?
o: fast is better: finishing is the whole point of reading.
slow is holier, so the slowest pace is always the best.
the pace you can keep: patience is the bow, and steady gets there.
games.why: Farid doesn't rank fast or slow; he makes patience the bow, the string and the arrow. the right pace is the one that lasts.

practice: Name your wish: a pace, a page a day, or a few lines. Name the one thing most likely to get in its way, a late night, a rushed morning. Then name your plan for it, like: if the night runs late, I'll read one line instead.
Say all three quietly, and let the breath settle around the plan.

wordCard.voice: The pace of a sehaj path: how much of the Granth you read each day; a page a day takes just under four years, five a day under one. The fifteenth word of the year.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Ang, the word used for the pages of the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: page by page. Drops fill the pot, and patience is the bow. Fifteen, steady.

sources.ref: Salok Sheikh Farid (Ang 1384: sabar manjh kamaan e, sabar ka neehano, sabar sanda baan, khaalak khataa na karee), paraphrased

sources.q: Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled

sources.ref: the standard printed saroop of the Guru Granth Sahib, Angs 1–1430 (the last Ang is numbered 1430); the outline's line on pace
